analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to cover follow-up care for mothers and newborns sent home from the hospital early after childbirth.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by a bipartisan group of 54 House members, never got a vote and died in committee at the end of the 105th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: In the late 1990s, insurers were pushing hospitals to send mothers and newborns home within a day or two of birth to save money. A 1996 federal law guaranteed minimum hospital stays, but if a mother and her doctor agreed to go home sooner, nothing required her insurance to pay for follow-up care afterward. This bill would have required group health plans and insurers to cover a home visit or office visit by a nurse, doctor, or midwife within 72 hours of any early discharge, with the mother choosing the setting and the provider. It never received a vote in any committee or on the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: New mothers and their newborns covered by group or individual health insurance. If they leave the hospital early after a vaginal or cesarean delivery, their insurer would have to pay for timely post-delivery care — a home visit, clinic visit, or provider visit within 72 hours — selected by the mother and delivered by a registered nurse, physician, nurse practitioner, nurse midwife, or physician assistant experienced in maternal and child health.

how_it_helps.text: When a mother and her attending provider decide on an early discharge, the group health plan or insurer must cover timely post-delivery care within 72 hours, in a setting the mother selects: her home, a provider's office, a hospital, a federally qualified health center, a rural health clinic, or a state maternity clinic.

The covered care must be provided by a registered nurse, physician, nurse practitioner, nurse midwife, or physician assistant experienced in maternal and child health, and must include appropriate monitoring of the mother's and baby's conditions.
The requirement applies to both group health plans and coverage sold in the individual market, so it protects women who buy insurance on their own as well as those with employer coverage.
The rules were set to take effect for plan years beginning after January 1, 1999, with a phase-in for plans governed by existing collective bargaining agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer-sponsored health plans, which would bear the cost of the new mandatory coverage. That cost would ultimately be reflected in premiums paid by employers and workers, though the mandate applies only when an early discharge occurs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: Mandated benefits add to insurance costs. Insurers and employers generally oppose federal coverage mandates on the grounds that each requirement raises premiums, which workers and employers pay; this bill imposes a new required benefit on all group and individual plans.

The bill does not require insurers to pay for a longer hospital stay in the first place; an insurer could still push for an early discharge so long as it then pays for a follow-up visit, leaving the burden of travel and care logistics on the new mother.

Because the requirement rides on three federal statutes covering group plans, individual plans, and the tax code, it overrides differences among state benefit rules, a one-size-fits-all approach some states would have preferred to set themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and targeted: a covered check-up for every mother and newborn sent home within 48 hours of a vaginal delivery or 96 hours after a cesarean, at what most analyses of such mandates treat as a small per-premium cost. The main honest objection is that federal mandates raise premiums slightly for everyone, and the bill's remedy addresses symptoms of early discharge rather than stopping insurers from pushing it. On balance the protection is modest in cost and real in value, and the bill attracted broad bipartisan sponsorship despite its relatively narrow scope.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with bipartisan support, referred to three House committees, and sent to subcommittees, where it sat with no markup, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steven LaTourette, a Republican, introduced the bill on November 6, 1997, joining 32 original cosponsors from both parties.

The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and additionally to the Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means committees, splitting its provisions among three panels with separate jurisdictions.
Within three weeks it was sent to subcommittees — Health, Health and Environment, and Employer-Employee Relations — and no further action was ever recorded.

By the time the bill gathered 53 cosponsors (44 Democrats, 8 Republicans, and 1 Independent), the session had passed the point where a multi-committee bill could move, and it died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans benefited, because they avoided a new federal mandate to cover post-delivery follow-up care. New mothers and newborns lost the guaranteed covered follow-up visit the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers avoided the coverage mandate

for.name: Rep. Steven C. LaTourette
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require coverage of post-delivery follow-up care after early discharge.

for.name: Rep. Bernie Sanders
for.role: Cosponsor, the chamber's only Independent at the time

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee vote on the bill; after subcommittee referral in November 1997, no action was recorded for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split across party lines in both directions: a Republican sponsor and 8 Republican cosponsors joined 44 Democrats and 1 Independent, with no party opposing on the record — the bill died without a vote rather than losing one.

industries.note: The bill would have required insurers and employer plans to pay for a follow-up visit after every early post-birth discharge, a new mandatory benefit. Insurers routinely opposed such federal mandates as premium cost increases; the requirement also applied to coverage they sold directly in the individual market.

By guaranteeing coverage for post-discharge care in the mother's home or a provider's office, the bill would have created paying demand for registered nurses, nurse midwives, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants experienced in maternal and child health.

Employer-sponsored plans would have had to absorb the new required benefit, with a phase-in for plans under existing collective bargaining agreements. Many employers pass mandate costs to workers through premiums, so workers would share the burden.
